newsitem.title: FRANCE: French tax plan backed before journalists strike.
newsitem.headline: French tax plan backed before journalists strike.

text.p: On the eve of a national strike by journalists, a French parliamentary committee on Wednesday backed plans to scrap tax breaks for journalists and about 100 other professions.

The finance committee of the National Assembly (lower house) adopted plans to phase out the tax privileges, which amount to a 30 percent income tax deduction to cover journalists' professional expenses.
The committee also voted to trim the value-added tax on the media, saying it hoped to offset the journalists' losses by providing an extra subsidy for their employers.
Gaullist deputy Philippe Auberger said the scrapping of the tax breaks for professionals would earn the state two billion francs ($400 million).

Lowering the value-added tax rate on the media to two percent during 1998 and to 1.9 percent beginning in 1999 from the current 2.1 percent would cost the state about 100 million francs ($20 million), said deputy Charles de Courson of the centrist Union for French Democracy, who drafted the proposal.
Journalists' unions have called their second one-day strike this month on Thursday to protest against the plan to end the tax break, saying it is effectively part of a journalist's salary.

The full National Assembly will debate the plan on Monday as part of the 1997 budget bill. Last month's stoppage hit public broadcasters and news agencies, and many newspapers failed to appear the following day.
The other professions affected by the plans are wide-ranging and include flight crews and fashion models.
The government plans to phase out the journalists' deduction over five years along with dozens of other breaks for various professions, in a reform cutting income tax for most taxpayers.

French railway workers went on strike in parts of southern France bringing services to northeast Spain to a standstill. They were protesting against job cuts planned in the reorganisation of the loss-making state railway company SNCF.
